chunks: First: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). Second: What Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn Isa, from Shu'ayb, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who sold goods to another, and the buyer took possession of the goods but did not pay the price, then the buyer died while the goods were still in their original state: the goods are returned to the seller, and the creditors do not have the right to detain (compel) him. There is no contradiction in this report. Second: He was asked about a man who had a partnership (mudarabah), a deposit, or orphans' funds and merchandise, and he owed money to people as a loan. He died leaving one thousand dirhams or more, but his debts to people were more than what he left. He said: The assets are distributed among all those creditors proportionally according to their shares. Because the first report only applied when the item was still in its original state, it is returned to its owner and the creditors do not detain it. The second report merely states he left a specific amount with debts. He said they are distributed by shares. There is no contradiction between the two reports. The ruling to rely upon is what we cited in the Book of Debts: the goods are returned to their owner only if the deceased left enough to pay the debts of the others besides them. But if he left only those specific goods, the owner of the goods is equal to the remaining creditors, and they are distributed equally.
ai.seo_question: How are debts distributed if the deceased sold goods but died before paying, and the goods are still in the buyer's possession?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent conflict between two reports by distinguishing between specific goods remaining intact, which revert to the seller, and general assets, where the seller ranks equally with other creditors. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that unpaid sales do not grant the seller priority over general debts unless the specific item is preserved, ensuring equitable distribution among all claimants.
